Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

issues.item: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: This strategy is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The trigger, threat, and memory items all center on intrusive reliving, bodily/sensory cues, and generalized danger/safety monitoring after terrorism, but nothing else points specifically to vehicles or transport-related threat. For a terrorism trauma this is possible, but without any corresponding trigger, memory, or threat content linked to cars/roads/passenger situations, this item stands out as a likely incoherent addition rather than part of the same formulation.

vignette:
María Elena is a 44-year-old Latina woman, divorced, who has spent the last several years in religious life as a nun. Before entering the convent, she had already lived through the painful upheaval of a marriage ending, and she describes having sought a life of service and structure afterward. The event that now dominates her inner life occurred during a public religious gathering she attended with other sisters, an event held in a crowded civic plaza where worshippers, families, and tourists stood shoulder to shoulder. She remembers the day first as heat, noise, and press of bodies, and then as abrupt terror when an explosion tore through the crowd. In the moments that return to her now, she does not recall it as a narrative but as a total sensory assault: the blast, the force through her body, the metallic smell, people screaming, and the sight of blood on the ground and on clothing. She sustained a painful injury during the attack, and the pain in that same part of her body still has a special power over her. When it flares unexpectedly, she is no longer simply noticing discomfort; she is thrust back into that plaza with a certainty that the danger is present again.

In the weeks afterward, María Elena found that the memory did not come when she chose it. Instead it forced itself into her mind in fragments so vivid that she felt she was reliving the attack across all her senses at once. Blood was especially potent. A small cut in the convent kitchen, blood drawn at a medical appointment, even seeing red on fabric could bring a rush of horror that felt immediate rather than remembered. Night brought little relief. She began waking from nightmares already gripped by the atmosphere of the attack, as if she had surfaced from sleep but not fully left the scene. In those moments before dawn, lying in her small room at the convent, she would sit upright and orient herself to the crucifix, the dresser, the window, trying to convince herself she was here and not there. Yet if the old injury was aching at the same time, she could feel overtaken all over again.

What has unsettled her almost as much is that when she tries to remember the event deliberately, to tell it in order or pray through it, the memory becomes strangely inaccessible. She can be flooded by it without warning, but if she sits with a therapist or spiritual director and tries to recount exactly what happened from beginning to end, parts disappear. This has left her going over the details repeatedly in her own mind, searching for coherence, revisiting where she had been standing, where others were standing, what she saw before and after the blast, as if enough review might finally make it settle into something she can understand. Instead, the process leaves her exhausted, frightened, and no more certain.

Over the months, María Elena's world narrowed. She came to feel safe only in a very limited set of places: her room, the chapel when nearly empty, and a few quiet corners of the convent. Outside those spaces she rarely relaxed. If she had to accompany other sisters to Mass at a larger parish, to a hospital ministry, or even to a grocery store, she found herself immediately scanning for exits before she could feel remotely settled. She noticed doors, side aisles, stairwells, the width of hallways, who was blocking which path. Crowds became especially difficult. In dense public places she felt trapped, as if the same kind of sudden catastrophe could happen again and she would not be able to get out. She increasingly declined outings that involved festivals, public prayer services, or busy stores, which changed how the community included her and limited parts of her ministry.

She has also become more emotionally removed from other people. Life in a convent ordinarily involves a closeness of daily routine, shared prayer, and mutual reliance, but María Elena has pulled back from being known too well. She keeps conversations practical, avoids lingering after meals, and turns aside gentle attempts by other sisters to ask how she is really doing. What frightened her most about closeness was not simply being upset in front of others; it was the sense that if she let herself open, the whole terror would spill out in an uncontrolled way. Strong feelings arrive quickly for her now-fear most of all, but also anger, guilt, shame, and a horror she finds difficult to name in religious language. She worries that others will see how shaken she remains and that she ought, by now, to be stronger.

She finally sought help after waking from another nightmare and finding herself unable to return to sleep before morning prayers. Later that same day, while assisting in the infirmary, she saw blood from a minor wound and had to leave abruptly, overcome by the feeling that the attack was happening again. The incident left her shaken and embarrassed in front of the other sisters. Coming to treatment, María Elena says she wants "some peace" and to stop living as though danger is waiting just outside a very small circle of safety. At the same time, she is afraid that speaking about the attack will make it more real, that once the memory opens it will come in all at once and she will be back in the plaza with no way out.
